title: Oldcastle Building Products Canada (Aug 2016 TCC) Case
subject: TCC appeal on whether an executive's sales-based variable salary was an eligible SR&ED salary under the proxy method.
summary: Oldcastle Building Products Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2016 TCC 183, is a Tax Court of Canada SR&ED ruling for corporations claiming under the Income Tax Act. It held an executive's sales-based variable salary was neither a bonus nor profit-based remuneration, so the portion tied directly to R&D (55% in 2010, 40% in 2011) qualified under the proxy method.
metaDescription: Analyze the August 2016 Tax Court of Canada decision for Oldcastle Building Products Canada Inc. on SR&ED tax credits.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary and Background of the Case
Factual Background and Nature of the Taxpayer's Claim

The case Oldcastle Building Products Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2016 TCC 183 (Court File No. 2014-3152(IT)G), decided on August 25, 2016, by the Honourable Justice Pierre Archambault of the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) under the general procedure, constitutes a landmark precedent in Canadian tax jurisprudence on the tax incentive program for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED). The appellant, Oldcastle Building Products Canada Inc., is a Canadian corporation forming part of an international building products group based in Ireland, CRH Group, whose worldwide revenue amounts to approximately $30 billion; in 2001, a company in this group acquired, for more than $100 million, Groupe Permacon, one of whose founding companies was Bloc Vibré inc., a Sherbrooke-based business that had belonged to the family of Mr. Bertin Castonguay. According to the reasons for judgment, Oldcastle is a North American leader in the manufacture of concrete products for masonry and landscaping, as well as retail products for do-it-yourself construction and landscaping.

As part of its manufacturing operations, Oldcastle Building Products Canada Inc. filed claims for SR&ED expenditure deductions and investment tax credits (ITCs) using prescribed form T661. These claims, covering the 2010 and 2011 taxation years, related to R&D projects carried out by Oldcastle's Research Centre — a facility built in Ville d'Anjou (Montréal) at a cost of six to seven million dollars, employing between 25 and 30 employees from 2004 to 2012 and dedicated to the development of new products and new processes — whose eligibility itself was not at issue before the Court. Oldcastle had elected the proxy method provided in clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the Income Tax Act (ITA), and the expenditure component remaining in dispute concerned solely the remuneration of Mr. Bertin Castonguay, President of the Research Centre, whose "variable salary" was calculated as a percentage of net sales of the new or modified products developed by the Centre.
Challenge by the Tax Authority (Canada Revenue Agency)

The Minister of National Revenue, through the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), issued assessments for the 2010 and 2011 taxation years that refused to treat Mr. Castonguay's salary as an R&D expenditure for the purposes of section 37 ITA and the calculation of the ITC, on the ground that his activities were not directly related to the R&D activities of the reviewed projects, and that set the appellant's proxy amount at zero. The assessments also raised other issues — including the refusal, for 2010, of a capital R&D expenditure of $22,850 on the ground that it had been incurred only in 2011 — which the parties settled before the hearing of the appeals, the scientific and technological eligibility of the R&D projects themselves not being at issue.

On the scientific and technical side, the respondent did not dispute the eligibility of the reviewed R&D projects: the Court expressly notes that the eligibility of the projects themselves is not at issue, and the reasons address neither standard engineering practice, nor trial and error, nor technological uncertainty or advancement within the meaning of subsection 248(1) ITA. Moreover, following meetings between Mr. Castonguay and CRA representatives, the respondent acknowledged, in a letter dated July 4, 2016, and then at the outset of the hearing, that 55% of Mr. Castonguay's working hours in 2010 and 40% in 2011 were directly related to the R&D activities of the reviewed projects.

On the financial and expenditure compliance side, the Crown disputed only the characterization of Mr. Castonguay's remuneration, whose employment contract described as a "bonus" the component calculated on the basis of net sales of new or modified products, and which totalled $1,058,000 in 2010 and $1,114,000 in 2011, his base salary then being nil under clause 10.6 of that contract. The CRA essentially argued that this variable salary did not constitute an expenditure described in section 37 ITA because the calculation formula referred to the sale of products in respect of which R&D activities had been carried out in previous years, so that it could not be remuneration for the R&D activities carried out by Mr. Castonguay during the relevant years; the Court also had to determine whether this remuneration constituted a "bonus" or "remuneration based on profits" excluded by subsection 2900(9) of the Income Tax Regulations (ITR).
Applicable Legislative, Regulatory and Jurisprudential Framework in Canada

The Tax Court of Canada's analysis in Oldcastle Building Products Canada Inc. falls within the rigorous architecture of the Income Tax Act (R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) and the Income Tax Regulations (ITR). The Canadian SR&ED tax regime rests on a sequential normative structure that requires, first, the scientific characterization of the work under subsection 248(1) ITA and, second, the strict connection of the expenditures incurred under section 37 ITA and section 2900 ITR.

Under subsection 248(1) ITA, which codifies the definition formerly found in subsection 2900(1) ITR, "scientific research and experimental development" means a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology carried out by means of experiment or analysis. For manufacturing businesses such as Oldcastle, the characterization rests essentially on paragraph 248(1)(c) ITA, which covers "experimental development", namely work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement to create new, or improve existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Once these core activities are established, paragraph 248(1)(d) ITA allows the inclusion of work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing and psychological research, but only to the extent that such work is "directly in support of" the work described in paragraphs 248(1)(a), (b) or (c) and is "commensurate with the needs" of that work. In contrast, paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k) ITA expressly exclude several routine activities, including quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products or processes, commercial production of a new or improved material, device or product, commercial use of a new or improved process, as well as market research and style changes.

The judicial interpretation of the definition in subsection 248(1) ITA is governed by the classic five-criteria test formulated in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC), whose authority remains constant before the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal. This analytical framework requires the taxpayer to demonstrate, on a balance of probabilities, first, the existence of a scientific or technological risk or uncertainty that cannot be removed by the mere application of basic knowledge or standard, routine engineering practice. The taxpayer must then prove the formulation of hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty, followed by the adoption of a procedure consistent with the scientific method, including systematic observation, testing of hypotheses by means of experiment or analysis, and modification of hypotheses based on the results obtained. In addition, the approach must aim to achieve a technological advancement arising from the experimental process, regardless of the commercial success or failure of the project, and must be accompanied by detailed records of the hypotheses, tests and results kept as the work progresses.

On the financial side, subsection 37(1) ITA allows the deduction of expenditures of a current nature incurred in Canada for SR&ED activities, while subsection 37(8) ITA delimits eligible expenditures depending on whether the taxpayer chooses the "traditional method" (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) ITA) or the "proxy method" (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) ITA). Under the proxy method, only the salaries or wages of employees "directly engaged in SR&ED" enter into the salary base used to calculate the prescribed proxy amount (PPA) and the investment tax credits provided under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) ITA. Under the traditional method, the salaries or wages of employees who directly undertake, supervise or support the performance of SR&ED are eligible, while directly attributable administrative salaries fall under overhead. Finally, subsection 37(11) ITA strictly governs the terms and deadlines for filing prescribed form T661; as for the limits examined in detail in the reasons, subsection 37(9) ITA excludes remuneration based on profits and bonuses only for "specified employees", subsection 37(9.1) ITA caps the eligible salary of the latter at five times the year's maximum pensionable earnings, subsection 2900(4) ITR set the proxy amount, for the 2010 and 2011 taxation years, at 65% of the salaries of employees directly engaged in R&D (a rate since reduced to 55%), and subsection 2900(9) ITR excludes, for any employee, bonuses and remuneration based on profits from the calculation of that amount.
Final Decision and Conclusions of the Tax Court of Canada

Justice Pierre Archambault allowed the appeals of Oldcastle Building Products Canada Inc. for the 2010 and 2011 taxation years and referred the assessments back to the Minister of National Revenue for reconsideration and reassessment on the basis that 55% of Mr. Castonguay's variable salary incurred in 2010 and 40% of that incurred in 2011 constitute expenditures described in section 37 ITA and in the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) ITA, as well as expenditures for the purposes of calculating the proxy amount under subsection 2900(4) ITR, that Oldcastle is entitled to a proxy amount based on the data provided to the CRA, and that the capital expenditure of $22,850 is allowable for the 2011 taxation year, with the fixing of costs deferred to a later date. The decision establishes three major guiding principles, all relating to the characterization of remuneration for SR&ED purposes; it does not address the scientific eligibility of the work, non-specialized employees or contemporaneous documentation, matters that fall instead under subsection 248(1) ITA, the Northwest Hydraulic case law and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy. First, the Court held that Mr. Castonguay's variable salary is not a "bonus" within the meaning of the ITA and the ITR, since it is not an amount paid at the employer's discretion in addition to what is owed: it is payable under the terms of the employment contract and constituted, in 2010 and 2011, Mr. Castonguay's sole remuneration, his base salary having become nil. Second, the Court ruled that this remuneration is not "remuneration based on profits" either, since the formula is based on the sales of products developed by the Research Centre, reduced by only two expenses, namely transportation and insurance costs, so that too many expenses are missing to determine whether Oldcastle was making a profit; nor is it a commission, a royalty or remuneration for services rendered in previous years. Third, the judgment specifies that the CRA confuses the method of calculating remuneration with its nature: the variable salary remunerated the work performed by Mr. Castonguay during the year as President of the Research Centre, so that, under the proxy method, the portion of that salary corresponding to the time he spent directly on R&D (55% in 2010 and 40% in 2011, according to the CRA's admissions) is eligible, without a cap, since Mr. Castonguay — who held no shares of Oldcastle or CRH Group and dealt at arm's length with his employer — was not a specified employee.
2. Fundamental Legal and Evidentiary Failures

The detailed analysis of Justice Archambault's reasons in Oldcastle Building Products Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2016 TCC 183) reveals no legal, technical or documentary failure on the part of the taxpayer: the Court ruled in Oldcastle's favour, and the themes examined below fall under the general SR&ED framework rather than the conclusions of this judgment, which addressed only the characterization of Mr. Castonguay's variable salary. These issues, which were not argued in the Oldcastle case, illustrate in general terms the gap that can separate the industrial management of manufacturing innovation from the legal requirements of the Income Tax Act.
Failure to Prove Technological Uncertainty and the Point at Which It Concretely Arises

The Court identified no inability on the taxpayer's part to establish the existence of technological uncertainty, since the eligibility of Oldcastle's R&D projects was not at issue; the requirement of genuine technological uncertainty distinct from routine engineering challenges and commercial performance objectives nevertheless remains a general principle of the regime. In the precast concrete products industry, the design of a new masonry block or architectural paver, or the modification of a moulding line, inevitably involves technical unknowns related to compressive strength, freeze-thaw cycles, efflorescence, demoulding time or vibro-compaction rate. However, as the case law stemming from Northwest Hydraulic points out, a technical difficulty or uncertainty about achieving a commercial objective or a target cost does not in itself constitute "scientific or technological uncertainty" within the meaning of subsection 248(1) ITA.

Technological uncertainty exists in Canadian tax law only when the probability of achieving a given objective, or the way to achieve it, cannot be known or determined on the basis of the generally available state of scientific or technological knowledge or the normal experience of competent specialists in the field. In the Oldcastle file, however, the evidence submitted to the Tax Court judge did not concern the nature of the technical work, the CRA having acknowledged that Mr. Castonguay — holder of 72 patents — devoted 55% (2010) and 40% (2011) of his working hours directly to the R&D activities of projects whose eligibility was not disputed.

A taxpayer cannot retroactively include all preliminary planning stages, feasibility studies, standard mechanical design and initial assembly of equipment under the SR&ED label merely because an unforeseen technological obstacle later emerged during start-up testing. As long as the engineer applies standard practice and the limit of existing technological knowledge has not been concretely reached in the field, the work remains ineligible routine engineering.
Absence of a Structured Experimentation Process and Confusion with Trial-and-Error Methodology

The second theme, which was also not argued in Oldcastle, concerns the general requirement to prove the existence of a "systematic investigation or search [...] carried out by means of experiment or analysis" in accordance with subsection 248(1) ITA. To satisfy the second and third Northwest Hydraulic criteria, the taxpayer must demonstrate that it formulated explicit scientific or technological hypotheses establishing a causal relationship between manipulated parameters and a poorly understood physical, chemical or mechanical phenomenon, and then subjected these hypotheses to rigorous testing protocols followed by analyses.

In a concrete plant environment, changes to aggregate mixes, chemical admixtures or moulding press settings may be made pragmatically and empirically, but the Oldcastle decision contains no finding of this kind regarding the work of Oldcastle's Research Centre. For example, when a surface or mechanical strength defect is found on a series of blocks, technicians may successively modify various operating parameters, such as moisture content, vibration time or hydraulic pressure, until a commercially acceptable product is obtained. The general case law of the Tax Court of Canada — and not the Oldcastle decision, which does not address this issue — distinguishes this trial-and-error approach (trial and error) from systematic experimental development. Whereas the trial-and-error approach aims only to find a working configuration empirically by varying known parameters intuitively or sequentially, without seeking to understand or model the underlying technological laws, systematic experimentation requires the prior formulation of a precise causal hypothesis, strict control of independent variables, the collection of quantitative data commensurate with the needs of the analysis, and the deduction of conclusions that advance the company's technological knowledge base. In the Oldcastle case, however, the Research Centre's activities were never equated with industrial troubleshooting or routine tuning of production equipment, the eligibility of the R&D projects not being at issue.
Disqualification of Salaries or Wages, Direct Support and Work of Non-Specialized Employees

The jurisprudential contribution of Oldcastle Building Products Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2016 TCC 183) relates to the tax treatment of the variable remuneration of an R&D executive — and not that of plant employees or non-specialized staff, which the decision does not address. Under clauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and (B) ITA, the deductibility of salaries and their inclusion in the calculation of the PPA under the proxy method, or in direct expenditures under the traditional method, require that the portion of salary claimed correspond strictly to the time during which the employee is "directly engaged in SR&ED" or directly undertakes, supervises or supports those activities. In the Oldcastle case, the only salary at issue was that of Mr. Bertin Castonguay, President of the Research Centre and Chair of the Board of Directors of Oldcastle, whose employment contract provided, after the first three years, for a base salary of $100,000 reduced by $20,000 for each $100,000 of "bonus" exceeding $500,000, as well as a variable salary calculated according to declining percentages of annual net sales of "New Products" (from 1.5% to 0.125%) and "Modified Products" (from 0.30% to 0.10%).

Justice Archambault sets out no condition regarding non-specialized employees; rather, it is the CRA's administrative guidelines, in particular section 7.1.1 of its SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, that set out strict cumulative conditions for the time of a non-specialized employee to be considered as spent directly on SR&ED. First, no support work described in paragraph 248(1)(d) ITA can be characterized as SR&ED unless it is directly related to a duly proven activity of pure research (paragraph (a)), applied research (paragraph (b)) or experimental development (paragraph (c)). Second, since non-specialized workers such as concrete press operators or assembly line workers do not themselves carry out the scientific process, only the time spent by a non-specialized employee participating in an SR&ED project to perform work listed in paragraph 248(1)(d) ITA — in particular carrying out experiments, tests and analyses or collecting data — is eligible, on the express condition that such work is performed directly in support of and forms an integral part of the research or experimental development work.

Third, the volume of testing and the labour time claimed must be strictly commensurate with the needs of the experimentation and analyses. If verifying a technological hypothesis requires the manufacture of only a limited number of samples, continuing manufacturing over a full shift constitutes commercial production excluded by paragraph 248(1)(i) ITA, making the operators' salaries for that excess time entirely ineligible. Fourth, the support work performed by the non-specialized employee must imperatively be supervised by personnel with scientific or technological qualifications. Finally, as tax doctrine points out — and not the Oldcastle decision, in which the percentages of time spent directly on R&D (55% and 40%) were established by the CRA's admission — although prescribed form T661 does not provide a specific grid requiring a daily breakdown of each employee's tasks upon initial filing of the return, the taxpayer remains legally required, during a review or an appeal before the TCC, to prove in granular fashion the exact nature of the tasks performed and the actual time spent by each individual on eligible activities.
Insufficient Contemporaneous Documentation and Rejection of Retrospective Estimates

Oldcastle's appeal was allowed and the decision identifies no weakness in the contemporaneous documentary evidence, whether technical or relating to time tracking; the decisive evidence was Mr. Castonguay's signed employment contract (Exhibit A-4), which came into force on January 1, 2004, and was the ninth version of an agreement negotiated at length between parties dealing at arm's length. In accordance with the fifth Northwest Hydraulic criterion and the general record-keeping obligations of section 230 ITA, it is in the very nature of a systematic scientific investigation to generate written records as it unfolds, such as laboratory notebooks, dated experimental plans, test reports, compilations of measurements and minutes of failure analyses.

Before the TCC, however, at the hearing held on July 6, 2016, in Montréal, the debate focused not on project descriptions or testimony concerning the technical work, but on the interpretation of Mr. Castonguay's employment contract and the nature of his remuneration. The Tax Court judge assesses the evidence submitted before him, but does not rule on the jurisprudential principle that oral testimony given several years after the fact cannot make up for the absence of contemporaneous documents, as this issue does not arise in this case. Likewise, with respect to salary expenditures, the Court found no allocation of time percentages insufficient: it accepted the percentages of 55% (2010) and 40% (2011) admitted by the CRA and concluded that it was reasonable to apply these same percentages to Mr. Castonguay's variable salary, since it was the only salary he received from Oldcastle during the relevant years.
Development of Commercial Assets, Trial Production and Procedural Rules

The Oldcastle case does not address the legal pitfalls, which are nevertheless generally relevant, associated with SR&ED carried out in parallel with the development of an industrial asset (SR&ED while developing an asset) or during plant production. When a company designs or modifies a manufacturing machine in its plant or produces pilot batches of concrete blocks that are subsequently incorporated into inventory intended for sale, it exposes itself to the recharacterization of its work as ineligible commercial operations or capital asset engineering. In addition, on the procedural and tax litigation side before the Tax Court of Canada, a separate and later decision involving the same company — Oldcastle Building Products Canada Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2025 TCC 107, and not the 2016 judgment — highlights the strategic importance of the TCC's rules of procedure, such as section 58 of the Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure) for determining preliminary questions of law or admissibility, as well as the increased vigilance required by the legislative evolution of subsection 152(9) ITA allowing the Minister to raise new grounds or alternative arguments in support of an assessment up to the appeal stage.

The table below maps each of the general legal, regulatory and jurisprudential SR&ED requirements, considered in light of Oldcastle Building Products Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2016 TCC 183), against what the decision actually found or decided in their regard (no failure on the part of the taxpayer having been identified) and the standard of proof generally required by the Tax Court of Canada.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remediation Case Studies

In order to translate the jurisprudential lessons of Oldcastle Building Products Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2016 TCC 183) into operational tax compliance strategies, the following two case studies illustrate how Canadian manufacturing businesses facing general SR&ED legal pitfalls — distinct from the remuneration issue decided in Oldcastle — can restructure their governance, technical documentation, contracts and financial tracking to fully satisfy the requirements of the ITA and the TCC.
Case Study No. 1: Industrial Manufacturing of Ultra-High-Performance Concrete Masonry Products with Accelerated CO2 Curing
Industrial Context and Initial Vulnerabilities

BétonNovation Québec Inc., a Canadian manufacturer of architectural masonry blocks and precast pavers operating in Quebec, undertakes a major project aimed at replacing 45% of ordinary Portland cement in its dry-cast concrete mixes (zero-slump concrete) with activated metallurgical slags and a carbon dioxide injection process during the vibro-compaction and curing cycle. The commercial objective is to obtain a block conforming to CSA A165 that reaches its target compressive strength in less than 12 hours while reducing its carbon footprint.

In its initial configuration, the company makes classic SR&ED errors, which, however, were neither sanctioned nor even examined in Oldcastle Building Products Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2016 TCC 183). First, the company fails to delineate the start of SR&ED by claiming the entire project from day one, which includes the selection of carbon dioxide injection nozzle suppliers, the mechanical engineering drawings to modify the curing enclosure and the first standard calibration tests. Next, the team carries out empirical tests in commercial production by running 18 test series on the main production line during regular shifts; each test produces 4,000 blocks, of which 3,800 are sold to customers if their visual appearance is deemed acceptable, without any protocol isolating the thermodynamic and chemical parameters. Finally, on form T661 prepared under the proxy method, the company improperly claims plant labour by entering 40% of the plant manager's annual salary, 60% of that of two process engineers, and 25% of the salary of 12 non-specialized press operators and forklift operators on the basis of a mere retrospective year-end estimate.
Comprehensive Step-by-Step Restructuring Plan
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Staging Technological Uncertainty

To meet the doctrinal requirement (which does not stem from Justice Archambault's reasons) of identifying the precise moment when technological uncertainty concretely arises, BétonNovation Québec Inc. establishes a structured project governance based on decision gates (Stage-Gate), supervised by an internal scientific committee led by its chief materials engineer, a member of the Ordre des ingénieurs du Québec. During the initial routine engineering phases, the review of technical literature, the mechanical engineering for installing the carbon dioxide manifold and the first formulation tests based on admixture suppliers' charts are coded under a separate accounting cost centre (ING-STD-01), so that no hours or materials from this preliminary phase are charged to SR&ED.

The switch-over milestone to SR&ED occurs only when, during standard validation tests, an unforeseen phenomenon concretely arises: injecting carbon dioxide into the high-slag mix causes instantaneous surface carbonation that clogs the block's capillary porosity in less than 4 seconds, preventing the gas from diffusing to the core of the block and creating an internal stress gradient that systematically cracks the pieces upon demoulding. The scientific committee then prepares a dated and signed Technological Impasse Report demonstrating why Fick's diffusion models and known vibro-compaction practices cannot resolve the conflict between the mechanical density required for immediate demoulding and the gas permeability needed for the exothermic carbonation reaction. This report sets the exact opening date of the SR&ED project (RSDE-2026-CO2). Symmetrically, as soon as the correlation law between bimodal grading, the pore-forming surfactant and the carbon dioxide pressure pulsation is established and validated, the committee signs a Technological Resolution Certificate, switching all subsequent cycle-rate optimization and CSA certification activities to the commercial production account.
Step 2: Overhaul of Contemporaneous Technical Documentation in Accordance with the Northwest Hydraulic Criteria

In order to eliminate the appearance of empirical trial and error, each experimental iteration is subject to a Contemporaneous Experimental Protocol Sheet (FPEC) generated in a time-stamped electronic system before the test is launched in the plant. Each FPEC must formulate an explicit quantitative and causal hypothesis, such as hypothesis H-04 postulating that introducing a non-ionic air-entraining agent at a dosage of 0.05% by mass of binder, combined with a modulation of the vibration frequency between 50 Hz and 65 Hz, will create a network of interconnected micro-channels between 20 and 80 µm in diameter, making it possible to increase the depth of carbon dioxide penetration without reducing the initial modulus of elasticity below the critical threshold at demoulding. The sheet rigorously records the experimental plan (Design of Experiments), detailing the independent variables manipulated, the variables held constant (aggregate temperature, water/binder ratio) and the dependent variables measured by X-ray diffraction on cores, infrared thermography, phenolphthalein pH measurement and compressive strength tests at 12 hours, 24 hours and 28 days. Within 48 hours of the test, the responsible engineer completes the results analysis section, scientifically explaining the deviations observed and justifying the modification of the hypothesis for the next test.
Step 3: Restructuring Contractual Arrangements (Subcontractors and Equipment Suppliers)

To prevent payments made to third parties from being recharacterized as capital acquisitions or ineligible commercial services, BétonNovation Québec Inc. carries out a strict contractual separation when it engages a specialized Canadian engineering firm to modify the gas injection system and perform finite element modelling of multiphase diffusion. The company enters into, on the one hand, an Industrial Equipment Supply and Installation Contract covering the manufacture and physical installation of standard valves, piping and sensors, which is entirely excluded from the SR&ED claim, and, on the other hand, a Contract for Experimental Research and Development Services on Behalf of the Principal governed by subsection 37(1) and paragraph 248(1)(d) ITA. This second contract expressly stipulates that the work is performed in Canada by qualified engineers directly in support of project RSDE-2026-CO2, that BétonNovation Québec Inc. bears the entire financial and technical risk of the work through time-based billing with no guarantee of commercial results, that all intellectual property as well as the raw data and mathematical models belong exclusively to the principal from the moment of their creation, and that the subcontractor undertakes not to claim any ITC on its own behalf while providing invoices broken down by task, by engineer and by FPEC protocol reference.
Step 4: Granular Tracking of Experimentation, Non-Specialized Employees and Materials

To comply strictly — Oldcastle (2016 TCC 183) not addressing these issues — with the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, resource tracking is completely revised around the principle of proportionality to needs. Instead of producing 4,000 blocks per test, the scientific committee determines by statistical calculation that 120 blocks (i.e., 10 moulding boards) are sufficient to measure thermal repeatability and take destructive test specimens. The production line is therefore stopped, purged, used for exactly 45 minutes to produce the 120 experimental blocks — which are entirely destroyed or scrapped after analysis, eliminating any issue of commercial production sold — and then returned to normal production.

As for the tracking of non-specialized employees governed by paragraph 248(1)(d) ITA, the 3 plant operators who handle the mixer and the press during the 45-minute test clock in under the RSDE-SOUTIEN code only for the exact duration of preparing the experimental mix, moulding the 10 boards, collecting samples and the cleaning required by the test. Their daily electronic timesheet mandatorily requires the FPEC-04 protocol number, a precise description of the eligible task under paragraph 248(1)(d) ITA, and the electronic co-signature of the materials engineer present on the plant floor who directly supervised the test. Finally, the plant manager is removed from the claim for his administrative duties, and only the hours during which he acts as an engineer participating directly in hypothesis analysis meetings or in direct supervision in the field are counted, by means of detailed weekly timesheets to the nearest half-hour, after strict deduction of any leave or extended vacation periods.

body.text: Case Study No. 2: Development of a Robotic Hybrid Laser-Arc Assembly and Welding Cell with Real-Time Optical Feedback
Industrial Context and Initial Vulnerabilities

MécaSoudure Avancée Canada Ltée, an industrial equipment manufacturer established in Ontario and Quebec, designs and integrates, for its own manufacturing needs, a robotic cell capable of performing hybrid laser-arc (HLA) welding on aluminium-lithium alloy chassis of variable geometry. The project aims to develop in parallel the physical asset, namely the robotic cell, and a closed-loop adaptive control algorithm processing spectral images to suppress gas porosity and hot cracking in real time.

The initial vulnerabilities of the file illustrate general pitfalls — not addressed in Oldcastle Building Products Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2016 TCC 183) — regarding SR&ED carried out during the development of an industrial asset (SR&ED while developing an asset) and the justification of salaries. First, the company conflates the construction of the asset with experimental development by attempting to claim all the hours of its mechanical engineers, electrical engineers and programmable logic controller (PLC) programmers devoted to the mechanical architecture of the cell, safety wiring and the integration of commercial robotic arms. Second, the technical narrative submitted on form T661 describes the features of the complete cell rather than isolating the fundamental physical conflict between the plasma plume of hybrid welding, which saturates optical sensors in the near infrared, and the maximum latency allowed for modulating laser power before the weld pool solidifies. Third, machining technicians and welder-fitters not specialized in optical research spent hundreds of hours fabricating the cell's jigs and machining production parts, time that was included globally in the T661 salary claim without distinguishing between construction of the asset and direct support for experimental tests, and without filing prescribed agreement T1174 for a specified shareholder engineer working between two associated corporations of the group.
Comprehensive Step-by-Step Restructuring Plan
Step 1: Segregation Governance Between Capital Engineering and SR&ED

To prevent the overall disqualification of the project on the ground that it involves the development of a capital property or routine engineering, technical and tax management sets up a two-part governance architecture from the outset. The Work Breakdown Structure formally splits the capital investment project (CAPEX-CELL-2026) from the experimental development sub-project (RSDE-OPT-HLA), so that all mechanical engineering of the frames, standard robotic path programming, integration of safety controllers and industrial commissioning remain charged exclusively to the capital account.

The triggering of the SR&ED scope (RSDE-OPT-HLA) is authorized only after integration tests of commercial pyrometric sensors and CMOS cameras on a test bench have demonstrated the technological impossibility of simultaneously filtering the thermal radiation of the aluminium plasma and extracting the three-dimensional geometry of the capillary (keyhole) in less than 2 ms using existing image processing algorithms. This concrete manifestation of technological uncertainty is the subject of a dated Initial Technological Qualification Memorandum validated by the R&D director (Ph.D. in engineering physics).
Step 2: Technical Documentation Protocol and Algorithmic and Physical Traceability

To establish irrefutably the existence of a systematic investigation before the CRA or the TCC, each software and optical development branch in the Git repository is linked to a formal hypothesis documented in a contemporaneous technical register. By way of illustration, hypothesis H-12 states that discrete wavelet spectral decomposition applied only to the narrow emission band of evaporated magnesium, coupled with a Kalman predictive state model reduced to 4 degrees of freedom, will make it possible to reconstruct the keyhole collapse depth in less than 2 ms with a signal-to-noise ratio above 12 dB despite occlusion by the metal vapour plume. At the same time, each experimental welding test automatically generates a time-stamped telemetry file recording laser power, arc current and raw spectra, which is associated with the X-ray radiography report and micrographic cross-section of the welded sample, thus constituting the contemporaneous material evidence required by the fifth Northwest Hydraulic criterion.
Step 3: Contractual Framework for External Researchers and Compliance of Associated Corporations

When MécaSoudure Avancée Canada Ltée collaborates with a Canadian university research centre and a local optical integrator, the contractual agreements specify the exact breakdown of eligible costs incurred in Canada, the absence of undeducted government assistance under paragraph 37(1)(d) ITA, and the detailed Statement of Work describing only the experimentation and mathematical analysis tasks covered by subsection 248(1) ITA. No SR&ED subcontracting payment is authorized by the accounting department without the joint submission of the corresponding experimental analysis report and a detailed timesheet from the subcontractor isolating the hours of testing and modelling from the hours of hardware installation. Furthermore, with respect to the principal researcher, who is a "specified employee" holding at least 10% of the issued shares of a class and dividing his time between two associated corporations of the group, the legal department ensures that his eligible remuneration is limited to the cap of 5 times the year's maximum pensionable earnings (YMPE), that any bonus or remuneration based on profits is excluded, and that prescribed form T1174 is filed with the CRA, accompanied by a certified copy of the board of directors' resolution authorizing the salary allocation.
Step 4: Salary Allocation Mechanism and Strict Control of Technical Support

In accordance with the principles set out in sections 7.0 and 8.0 of the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy — and not in Oldcastle Building Products Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2016 TCC 183), which does not concern the allocation of working time — the company sets up a rigorous labour tracking matrix in its ERP system that blocks any generic entry. When a programmer codes the standard human-machine interface (HMI) of the robotic cell, he charges his time to the unclaimed CAPEX-IHM code; when he programs and tests the mathematical core of wavelet spectral filtering linked to hypothesis H-12, he charges his time to the RSDE-OPT-H12 code, attaching the identifier of the corresponding Git commit.

As for non-specialized welders and machinists, their time is entirely excluded when they fabricate the cell frame or perform standard calibration welds. On the other hand, when a technician prepares aluminium-lithium test plates instrumented with thermocouples, performs the experimental weld beads under the direct supervision of the engineering physics researcher and cuts the samples for destructive micrographic analysis, each hour is recorded under an Experimental Support Work Order (BTSE). This work order documents the exclusive connection to test H-12, the justification that the number of machined specimens (15 plates per test matrix) is strictly commensurate with the needs of the statistical analysis of variance (ANOVA), and the contemporaneous validation by the R&D director attesting to his direct scientific supervision.

headers: Risk of Disqualification under General SR&ED Principles (not drawn from Oldcastle, 2016 TCC 183)

cells: Mechanical engineers and roboticists
Global claim of design and commissioning time for the robotic cell (development of an asset).
Exclusive allocation to the CAPEX code until the optical uncertainty concretely arises; only experimentation hours H-01 to H-15 are charged to SR&ED.
Software programmers
Inclusion of user interface development and standard industrial PLC sequences.
Traceability through Git commits linked to the algorithmic hypotheses of real-time spectral filtering; complete exclusion of infrastructure and HMI code.
Welders and machinists (non-specialized employees)
Claim of a percentage of annual salary without proof of proportionality or qualified supervision.
Time-stamped work orders (BTSE) covering only the preparation and cutting of test specimens, co-signed by the supervising researcher (Ph.D.).
Materials consumed or transformed
Inclusion of robotic cell components or commercially sold chassis.
Claim limited to aluminium-lithium alloy plates and shielding gas consumed and destroyed during documented micrographic tests.

body.text: 5. Summary of Strategic Lessons and Conclusions

Oldcastle Building Products Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2016 TCC 183) remains a pillar of Canadian SR&ED tax jurisprudence, particularly regarding the characterization, for the purposes of section 37 ITA and the proxy amount, of variable remuneration calculated on the basis of sales of products resulting from R&D, which the Court held to be neither a bonus nor remuneration based on profits. Beyond this decision, practice shows that the durability of a claim for investment tax credits and deductions under section 37 ITA — both at the Canada Revenue Agency review stage and in litigation before the Tax Court of Canada — requires a rigorous integration of tax law and engineering governance.

First, the tax practitioner and the technical manager must surgically isolate the starting point of technological uncertainty, rejecting any approach that encompasses the complete commercial life cycle of an engineering or capital project. It is imperative to document in writing the precise moment when the state of the art and standard engineering practice failed, giving rise to a scientific or technological uncertainty that concretely arises for the first time. Second, in a plant context where the boundary between trial-and-error process optimization and experimental development is particularly porous, the characterization of the work under paragraph 248(1)(c) ITA rests entirely on the ability to produce contemporaneous protocols formulating explicit causal hypotheses and verifiable quantitative analyses aimed at a technological advancement distinct from the commercial property manufactured.

Third, in accordance with paragraph 248(1)(d) and subsection 37(8) ITA as interpreted in the CRA's administrative policies (Justice Archambault having instead interpreted, in Oldcastle, clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) ITA and subsection 2900(9) ITR with respect to the variable salary of an R&D executive), strict evidentiary discipline is required with respect to salaries or wages and non-specialized employees. No salary expenditure relating to non-specialized plant personnel can withstand judicial scrutiny without contemporaneous evidence that each hour claimed corresponds to an eligible task performed directly in support of and as an integral part of the experimentation, to an extent strictly commensurate with its needs and under the direct supervision of personnel with scientific or technological qualifications. Finally, the absolute contemporaneity of documentary evidence is the cornerstone of tax risk management in Canada: since narrative reconstructions written after the fact when preparing form T661 and retrospective estimates of percentages of working time lack sufficient probative value before the Tax Court of Canada, only governance that integrates the real-time capture of test data and activity-based timesheets guarantees the legal certainty of the tax incentives claimed.

outcome: Appeals allowed; the variable salary was not a bonus or profit-based pay, and 55% (2010) and 40% (2011) qualified.
